segments.text:
The comment gives the plan: 3 sessions, each with part A, part L and part C, then one more part C process.
- `whole-pass stop, 0.5 s` and `common stop, 6 s` name the stop rule and the time given with `--min-ms`. Part A uses `--min-ms 500` (in `ra.sh`). Parts L and C use `--min-ms 6000` (in the spec files) [Ref4].
- `old C read`, `new C read` and `asm read` are the old read kernel, the new read kernel and asmread.
- `like.spec` is equal to line 1 of `r8.spec`, an older spec file in the folder of `rx.sh` [Ref7].
- go.sh never reads `baselines-and-rules.txt`. Only this comment names it.
segments.heading: Header comment: the plan of the run

segments.text: `set -u`: the script stops when it uses a variable that was never set. The script does not use `set -e`. So a failed command does not stop it. Each check below calls `fail` by itself.

Paths on CRB and two expected checksums.
- `D`: the folder that holds `ra.sh` and the three spec files.
- `RX`: the runner script `rx.sh`. `BW`: the binary bwx12.
- `SHA`: the sha256 that the file bwx12 must have. `RXSHA`: the sha256 that `rx.sh` must have.
- Lines 22 and 23 test the two checksums.

`BOOT`: the boot id that the running system must have. Line 26 tests it. The comment gives the origin: the boot in which the file `try6.txt` recorded 12 memory modules at 7200 MT/s. That file holds this boot id [Ref5].

Prints one line that starts with `==` and the label given as argument. It only reports. It stops nothing. The line holds:
- the UTC time and the boot id
- the `MemTotal` line of `/proc/meminfo` (`tr -s ' '` reduces each run of spaces to one space)
- the content of `/proc/loadavg`: the three load averages, the runnable tasks and all tasks as `1/1013`, and the newest process id [Ref9]
- the number of logins: `who` prints one line per login, and `wc -l` counts the lines
- `present` or `absent` for the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`
- the number of processes of each user: `ps -eo user=` prints the user of every process, and `sort | uniq -c` counts equal lines
segments.heading: Function `state`: print one state line

segments.text: Prints `FAILED:` and the message. Then it prints a state line with the label `abort`. Then it ends go.sh with exit status 1. Every failed check of go.sh ends here, and no later step runs.
segments.heading: Function `fail`: stop the run

segments.text:
Prints the process id of go.sh and a command that stops the run.
- `kill -TERM -- -<pid>` sends the termination signal to every process of the process group with that number.
- This stops go.sh and its child processes only when go.sh is the leader of its process group. go.sh does not make itself the leader.
- In the rerun the start command ran go.sh through the tool `setsid` [Ref12]. This tool starts a program as the leader of a new process group [Ref13]. So go.sh was the leader in the rerun.

Check of the marker file.
- Test: does the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` exist.
- On failure (the file exists): `fail` stops the run with `RUNNING file present, Jeremy or someone else is using CRB`.
- The words after the comma were added on 2026-11-24, after the rerun [Ref18]. The text that ran had the message `RUNNING file present`. The rerun did not print it. Its log shows `marker absent` in all 12 state lines [Ref1].
- go.sh stops on the file only here. The function `state` (line 17) only reports the file as `present` or `absent`.
- `ra.sh` tests it again before each process [Ref2]. `rx.sh` tests it before each process and once per second while a process runs [Ref3].
- What the file stands for, by the message: Jeremy or someone else is using CRB. The word list says who Jeremy is. go.sh does not say who creates the file.
segments.heading: Checks before the run

segments.text:
Lock against a second run.
- `exec 9> ...` opens the file `go-T72.lock` for writing as file descriptor 9 of the shell. It creates the file when it is missing.
- Test: `flock -n 9` asks for an exclusive lock on that file and does not wait.
- On failure (another process holds the lock, or the lock file could not be opened): `fail` stops the run with `another go.sh holds the lock`.
- Purpose, by the message: no second go.sh may run at the same time. `go2.sh` uses the same lock file. So go.sh and go2.sh cannot run at the same time.
- The lock lasts as long as file descriptor 9 is open: until go.sh and the child processes that inherited it have ended.

Checksum checks of `rx.sh` (line 22) and of the binary bwx12 (line 23).
- Test: `sha256sum -c -` reads one line `checksum  path` from `echo`, computes the sha256 of that file and compares the two values. Its report goes to `/dev/null`, which discards it.
- On failure (the content differs, or the file cannot be read): `fail` stops the run.
- Purpose, by the messages: the two files must be the script and the binary of 2026-11-15.
- Cross-check: the build record of bwx12 lists the value of `SHA` for the file `bwx12` [Ref6]. The binary itself is not in the local folders. The local copy of `rx.sh` has the value of `RXSHA` (computed with `sha256sum` on 2026-11-21) [Ref3].

File checks.
- Line 24, test: `ra.sh` and the binary bwx12 exist and are executable (`-x`). On failure: `fail` with `not executable: <path>`.
- Line 25, test: `like.spec`, `cfwd.spec` and `crev.spec` exist and are not empty (`-s`). On failure: `fail` with `missing <path>`.
- go.sh does not test the checksum of `ra.sh` or of the spec files.
- `rx.sh` needs no execute permission. Line 31 starts it with `bash`.

Boot check.
- Test: the boot id of the running system is equal to `BOOT` (line 16).
- On failure: `fail` stops the run.
- Purpose, by the message and the comment in line 15: the run must happen in the boot that was checked at 12 modules and 7200 MT/s.
- The check compares the boot id only. It does not read the memory speed or the number of modules.

Memory size check.
- Test: `awk` prints the second field of the `MemTotal` line of `/proc/meminfo`, a value in kB. The value must be 395000000 kB or more.
- On failure: `fail` stops the run.
- Purpose, by the message: a lower value means `not 12 modules`. The script does not say how the limit was chosen.
- In the rerun each of the 12 state lines shows 395392808 kB [Ref1].

`rxok NAME` reads the file `launches.txt` of the newest result folder `w120-NAME-<time>`.
- `ls -d ... | tail -1` lists the matching files in name order and keeps the last one. The time in the folder name puts the newest folder last. `2>/dev/null` discards the error message of `ls` when no file matches.
- The function succeeds only when a file was found, the file holds exactly 1 line that starts with `rc `, and it holds exactly 1 line that starts with `rc 0 `.
- `rx.sh` writes one line `rc <exit status> <tag>` per process [Ref3].
- Reason, by the comment in line 28: `rx.sh` ends with status 0 also when bwx12 failed.
segments.heading: Function `rxok`: did the bwx12 process end with status 0

segments.text:
`runx NAME SPEC` runs one step of part L or part C.
- Line 31 starts `rx.sh` with `bash` and three arguments: NAME, the path of bwx12 and its expected sha256. The spec file is the input of `rx.sh` (`< "$2"`). go.sh waits until `rx.sh` has ended.
- On a non-zero exit status of `rx.sh`: `fail` stops the run and prints that status (`$?`).
- Line 32: when `rxok` (line 29) does not succeed, `fail` stops the run.
- Line 33 prints a state line with the label `after NAME`.
segments.heading: Function `runx`: one bwx12 process through `rx.sh`

segments.text:
Four lines for the log. None of them is a check.
- Line 35: the command line of the running Linux kernel.
- Line 36: the governor of each of the CPUs 0 to 119, counted per governor name. Then the file `scaling_cur_freq` of CPU 0, the current frequency that Linux reports for that CPU.
- Line 37: the settings `enabled` and `defrag` of transparent huge pages.
- Line 38: `taskset -cp $$` prints the CPUs on which this shell may run. go.sh does not set this list itself. The start command did not set it either [Ref12]. In the rerun the log shows `0-119` [Ref1].
segments.heading: Record of the machine settings

segments.text: State line with the label `start`.

Runs the sessions 1, 2 and 3, one after the other.
- Line 41, part A: `ra.sh T72A<s>` runs 24 processes of bw_old and bw_new, one kernel per process [Ref2]. On a non-zero exit status of `ra.sh`: `fail` stops the run. `ra.sh` uses `set -e`. So a process of part A that ends with a non-zero status ends `ra.sh` with that status [Ref2].
- Line 42: state line.
- Line 43, part L: one bwx12 process with the arguments of `like.spec`.
- Line 44, part C: one bwx12 process. Sessions 1 and 3 use `cfwd.spec`. Session 2 uses `crev.spec`, which holds the reverse kernel order.
- go.sh adds no pause between the steps. `ra.sh` waits once before its first process, and `rx.sh` waits before each process: until at most 2 tasks are runnable (at most 40 s), then 5 s [Ref2] [Ref3].
- When more than 2 tasks are still runnable after the 40 s, `ra.sh` ends with status 6 and go.sh stops. `rx.sh` starts its process anyway.
segments.heading: The three sessions

segments.text: One more part C process after session 3, with `crev.spec` and the name `T72C4`. Part C then has 2 processes in forward order (`T72C1`, `T72C3`) and 2 processes in reverse order (`T72C2`, `T72C4`). `T72C4` starts directly after `T72C3`. No part A and no part L run between them.
Final state line with the label `end`, then the word `ALLDONE`. The script reaches these lines only when no check called `fail`.
